decision_readiness.rationale: Classic HCL can be responsibly considered as the leading working hypothesis: 22% of mature B cells expressing CD19/CD20/CD22/CD11c/CD25/CD103 as well as BRAF V600E were recorded in the source. CD10 expression, defective κ/λ transcription, unclear cell-specific attribution of BRAF, and lack of morphological confirmation preclude definitive classification of the process or association of all bone and neurologic manifestations with it.

value.text: Complaints of periodic pain in the muscles of the proximal parts of the legs and arms, episodes of numbness of the chin and areas of the gums on the right, a feeling of generalized internal discomfort since the summer of 2023.

MRI of the brain from 05.2024 and MSCT of the skull from 02.2025: diffuse osteoporosis of the bones of the skull, more pronounced in the area of ​​the base of the skull, pyramids of the temporal bones, occipital bone; pathological bone marrow changes, considered as manifestations of a systemic process.

Immunophenotyping of bone marrow aspirate dated 11.12.2025: according to the results of immunophenotyping, a population of B-lymphocytes (~22%) with expression of CD19, CD20, CD10, CD22, CD11c, CD25, CD103, HLA-DR was detected.
Is there a predominance of the expression of light chains of immunoglobulins? (?/? ? 75%/25%).
The expression of markers T-cell, NK cell, myeloid and blast lines was not detected.
The presence of the BRAF V600E mutation was established by molecular genetic research.
General blood test from 11.12.2025: leukocytes – 6.3, erythrocytes – 4.93, hemoglobin – 149, hematocrit – 42.8, platelets – 254, neutrophils – 2.03 (32.2%), lymphocytes – 3.79 (60.2%), ESR – 47 mm/h.

General blood test from 05/19/2026: leukocytes – 5.36, erythrocytes – 4.57, hemoglobin – 144, hematocrit – 40.4, platelets – 215, neutrophils – 2.17 (40.5%), lymphocytes – 2.81 (52.4%), ESR – 54 mm/hour
MRI of the sacroiliac joints from 07/27/2026: MR image of widespread heterogeneous focal-diffuse bone marrow infiltration of the sacrum and iliac bones on both sides.
Given the anamnesis, the changes may primarily correspond to a specific bone marrow involvement (leukemic infiltration / leukemic deposits).
No convincing structural data for primary inflammatory sacrolith was found.

MRI of the brain from 05.2024 and MSCT of the skull from 02.2025: diffuse osteoporosis of the bones of the skull, more pronounced in the area of ​​the base of the skull, pyramids of the temporal bones, occipital bone; pathological bone marrow changes, considered as manifestations of a systemic process.

Is there a predominance of the expression of light chains of immunoglobulins? (?/? ? 75%/25%). The expression of markers T-cell, NK cell, myeloid and blast lines was not detected. The presence of the BRAF V600E mutation was established by molecular genetic research.
General blood test from 11.12.2025: leukocytes – 6.3, erythrocytes – 4.93, hemoglobin – 149, hematocrit – 42.8, platelets – 254, neutrophils – 2.03 (32.2%), lymphocytes – 3.79 (60.2%), ESR – 47 mm/h.

General blood test from 05/19/2026: leukocytes – 5.36, erythrocytes – 4.57, hemoglobin – 144, hematocrit – 40.4, platelets – 215, neutrophils – 2.17 (40.5%), lymphocytes – 2.81 (52.4%), ESR – 54 mm/hour

MRI of the sacroiliac joints from 07/27/2026: MR image of widespread heterogeneous focal-diffuse bone marrow infiltration of the sacrum and iliac bones on both sides. Given the anamnesis, the changes may primarily correspond to a specific bone marrow involvement (leukemic infiltration / leukemic deposits). narrative.text: In a 52-year-old man, the clinical history began with intermittent pain in the proximal muscles of the arms and legs, episodes of numbness of the chin and right gingival area, and generalized internal discomfort, which have continued since the summer of 2023. The combination of persistent muscle pain with a local sensory symptom in the mandibular area required evaluation of systemic bone involvement, bone marrow and a possible local process along the inferior alveolar nerve distribution. Such a symptom requires special attention due to possible bone or nerve damage.

MRI of the brain in May 2024 and multislice CT (MSCT) of the skull in February 2025 revealed a diffuse decrease in the density of the bones of the skull, especially in the base of the skull, petrous temporal bones and occipital bone, together with pathological bone marrow changes of a systemic nature. In July 2026, MRI showed widespread heterogeneous focal-diffuse bone marrow infiltration of the sacrum and both iliac bones; convincing signs of primary inflammatory sacroiliitis were absent. The distribution of changes confirms multifocality and determines the need to select a representative site for biopsy.

The complete blood count in December 2025 showed hemoglobin 149 g/L, platelets 254, white blood cells 6.3, and ESR 47 mm/h; in May 2026, the corresponding values ​​were 144 g/l, 215, 5.36 and 54 mm/h. There are no reference intervals for most of the indicators in the source, so these numbers describe longitudinal values without evaluating whether values are within reference limits. The rise in ESR remains a nonspecific sign of a systemic process. Leukocyte and platelet values ​​are also evaluated only within the limits of the recorded dynamics.

A key turning point occurred after the immunophenotyping of the bone marrow aspirate: about 22% of the cells were a mature B-cell population with CD19, CD20, CD22, CD10, CD11c, CD25, CD103 and HLA-DR, while molecular testing revealed BRAF V600E. This configuration pushed classic hairy cell leukemia to the fore, keeping splenic neoplasia, follicular lymphoma, plasma cell neoplasm, and aggressive B-cell lymphoma in the differential. Further ranking was based on the ability of each nosology to explain the leading clinical pattern.

Classic hairy cell leukemia is the leading hypothesis. The combination of CD11c, CD25 and CD103 in the mature B-cell population together with BRAF V600E most fully explains the hematological part of the picture and possible systemic bone marrow involvement. NCI reviews and the WHO-HAEM5 classification support the diagnostic significance of this phenotype and mutation. Trephine biopsy morphology, fibrosis, Annexin A1, CD123, and cell-specific attribution of BRAF remain crucial for definitive classification. These studies will also make it possible to match the hematological clone with bone manifestations.

Source comparison maintains HCL's leading position with clinically relevant caution. The NCCN algorithm for small cell mature B-cell neoplasm requires a combination of morphology, immunophenotype and molecular features; the CD103+/CD25+/CD11c+ branch predicts confirmation of CD123, Annexin A1, and BRAF. CD10 expression opens a separate verification of germinal center origin. A causal relationship between the B-cell population, bone foci, and chin numbness still requires tissue proof. Therefore, the imaging findings have a descriptive role; tissue verification remains decisive.

The second-ranked group comprises indolent splenic B-cell neoplasms — SBLPN, SMZL or SDRPL. They are close alternatives in the CD11c/CD103-positive population and bone marrow involvement. The WHO-HAEM5 classification considers these forms as separate nosologies, and the former HCL-v belongs to SBLPN. The expression of CD25 and BRAF V600E increases the likelihood of classic HCL, provided that both features belong to the same clone. Data on the spleen, monocytes and peripheral blood morphology are required. Molecular studies are performed according to the concordant morphologic pattern.

The third-ranked diagnosis is CD10-positive follicular lymphoma with bone marrow involvement. CD10 in mature B cells and the multifocal bone marrow process support this branch. The combination of CD11c, CD25, CD103 and BRAF V600E makes it substantially less concordant. Guidelines indicate the need to assess tissue architecture, BCL6, BCL2, IGH::BCL2 or t(14;18) and paratrabecular pattern. Biopsy of an accessible lesion should establish whether germinal center neoplasia is present. A single marker alone is not sufficient for diagnosis.

The fourth-ranked diagnosis is plasma cell neoplasm as a possible explanation for the dominant bone pattern, pain and numbness of the chin. Changes in the skull, sacrum, and iliac bones, along with an increase in ESR, require exclusion of multiple myeloma or plasmacytoma. The recorded cell population has a B-lymphocyte phenotype; the number and phenotype of plasma cells remain unknown. The diagnostic complex includes monoclonal protein, free light chains, calcium, renal function, whole-body imaging, and morphology. The availability of these data will allow comprehensive evaluation of myeloma criteria.

Aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma with bone, bone marrow or nerve involvement ranks fifth. Unilateral chin numbness and widespread bone marrow infiltration make this alternative critical for tissue exclusion. The long course, the HCL-like phenotype and the absence of blast markers reduce its concordance. The most informative accessible lesion requires histology, IHC and Ki-67; MYC, BCL2 and BCL6 are added for the corresponding morphology. PET/CT will help determine activity and optimal biopsy site.

A possible concomitant process in the skeleton, mandible, or bone metabolism is considered separately from the five ranked diagnoses. The B-cell clone may coexist with a local jaw lesion, metastatic, histiocytic, or metabolic disease. A unilateral sensory symptom and diffuse skull changes support the need for such an examination. A specific nosology is not defined here; its establishment depends on anatomical localization, biochemical indicators and histology of a representative bone lesion.

Another separate category concerns data quality and representativeness. The κ/λ record is corrupted, the primary FCS files and the cell population selection strategy are missing, the BRAF detection method, the proportion of the variant allele, and the cellular origin of the mutation are unknown. Because of this, the simultaneous expression of CD10 and HCL markers in one population remains unconfirmed. Technical review may change the classification, although the consistent combination of CD11c/CD25/CD103 with BRAF V600E reduces the likelihood of complete artifact.

The first diagnostic step is an expert review of the bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with morphology and IHC. In parallel, review of primary flow cytometry data, the exact κ/λ result, and distribution of CD10, CD11c, CD25, and CD103 among cell populations is needed. Orthogonal detection of BRAF in a well-defined population should link the mutation to the corresponding clone. Splenic findings, monocyte count, and peripheral blood morphology complete the distinction between HCL, SBLPN, SMZL, SDRPL, and follicular lymphoma.

emphasis_terms: the most informative site for biopsy
narrative.text: The second block of the examination is aimed at bone and neurological components. Full-body PET/CT, low-dose CT, or MRI should determine the distribution of lesions and the most informative site for biopsy. Tissue from the lesion should be compared with bone marrow findings by histology, IHC, flow cytometry, and BRAF. Persistent or progressive numbness, new cranial nerve deficits, local pain, swelling, or weakness require an urgent focused examination of the lower jaw and skull base.

An independent critique checked the relevance of the conclusions to the clinical facts, the completeness of the external supports, the preservation of critical alternatives, the calibration of the level of diagnostic confidence, and the linguistic quality. There are no critical or significant unresolved comments. The first five items are separately confirmed to be diagnostic hypotheses, a possible skeletal or jaw process has the role of a concomitant condition, and the uncertainty of flow cytometry, κ/λ, and BRAF belongs to the quality of the data. The clinician decision remains required.

The current summary supports classic HCL as the leading working hypothesis of the five ranked diagnoses. Final classification depends on morphology, IHC, primary flow cytometry data, and cell-specific attribution of BRAF. The origin of bone lesions and numbness of the chin requires a separate tissue and anatomical examination; plasma cell and aggressive lymphoid processes remain mandatory for exclusion. Staging, indications for treatment, and treatment regimen should be determined only after verification and recorded clinical judgment.
